title: The good point (Likutey Moharan 282)
hook: Rebbe Nachman: find the good point in another person, and in yourself, and it lifts them
tomorrow: an hour a day talking to God, in your own words. really?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tanya's wrestler: heaviness loses the match, joy gets the first move. Joy to wrestle. Today, a verse that sounds harsh, and a rebbe who found a song in it.

A screenshot of someone's worst moment can travel fast. One bad post, and that's who they are now. There's a verse in the Psalms that seems to agree. Psalm thirty-seven: a little while longer, and the wicked one is gone; you'll look closely at his place, and he isn't there. It reads like a promise that bad people simply vanish. Rebbe Nachman of Breslov read the same verse and heard hope, and something more: instructions. So what did he spot that the rest of us read straight past?
screen: `ONE BAD POST, AND THAT'S WHO THEY ARE.` → `THE WICKED ONE IS GONE?` → `WHAT DID HE SPOT?`

segments.voice: Two small Hebrew words near the start: od me'at, a little more, a little while. Rebbe Nachman reads them as: look for a little more. In the person who seems wholly wicked, find a little bit of good, a nekudah tovah, a good point. Something, somewhere, he did right. When you judge him by that point, he teaches in Likutey Moharan, teaching 282, you really do lift him toward the side of merit. Then the end of the verse comes true in a new way. You look at his place, and he isn't there. Not because he vanished, but because he's no longer standing where he was. That's the puzzle solved. The verse isn't about erasing a person. It's about finding the point that moves them. Then he turns it around, and this is the part people pass on. Do the same for yourself. When you look inside and see mostly failure, don't stop there. Search for one good point that's really yours, and then another. He ties it to a second verse, where the psalmist sings to God while he still has his being, and hears it as: with the little good still in me. Those good points, gathered one by one, he says, are like notes, and a melody is made from them. A teaching that starts with the worst person in the room ends as a song about you.
screen: `OD ME'AT: A LITTLE MORE.` · `FIND HIS GOOD POINT.` · `HE'S NO LONGER WHERE HE STOOD.` · `NOW FIND YOURS.` · then, large: `FIND THE GOOD POINT.`

segments.voice: Get a pen and a scrap of paper. Write the first name of someone you've written off lately, and next to it one good point that's really there, small is fine. Underneath, write one good point of your own, and let your eyes rest on both lines for the rest of the sit.
screen: `ONE NAME, ONE GOOD POINT.` · `THEN ONE OF YOURS.`

segments.voice: The good point: Rebbe Nachman's nekudah tovah. The bit of real good in a person, which, when you judge by it, lifts them, and you.
Here's the line: find the good point, in them first and then, harder, in you. That's today, done.

screen: `DAY 1612 COUNTS.` → `LATER VOICES · 5 OF 40.` → `TOMORROW: AN HOUR A DAY TALKING TO GOD, IN YOUR OWN WORDS. REALLY?`

howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim study Rebbe Nachman's teaching on the good point, known by its opening word Azamra, 'I will sing', and it is often taught as a way to judge others, and oneself, favorably.

fork.setup: your little brother broke your headphones and then lied about it. your parents ask what you think should happen. what would Rebbe Nachman's good point add?
options: name the lie, and also one real good thing you know is in him.
the lie is what matters now, so keep the focus there and only there.
let it go without a word, so nobody's mood gets worse tonight.
fork.reveal: Likutey Moharan 282 doesn't pretend the wrong away. it says judging a person by their good point lifts them toward merit.

original.note: Hebrew: a good point; Rebbe Nachman's phrase for the bit of good to look for in another person and in yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: find the good point means look on the bright side.
what it means: in Likutey Moharan 282, finding a little good in another person, and in yourself, and judging by it, lifts the person toward merit.
what a scholar hears: a reading of od me'at in Psalm 37:10 and of 'while I have my being' in Psalm 146:2, the good points gathered into a melody.

chat.meaning: Rebbe Nachman teaches that finding a person's good point and judging them by it actually lifts them toward merit. The notes can follow.

Rebbe Nachman of Breslov.meaning: a Hasidic master whose teachings fill Likutey Moharan

od me'at.meaning: a little more, a little while (Psalm 37:10)

nekudah tovah.meaning: a good point: the bit of real good in a person

Likutey Moharan.meaning: the collected teachings of Rebbe Nachman

sources.ref: Likutey Moharan I:282 (Azamra: find the good point in another, judge favorably, and he is lifted; then find good points in yourself; the good points make a melody)

notes: Likutey Moharan I:282 paraphrased: od me'at read as 'a little more' good; judging favorably lifts the person to the side of merit; 'you'll look at his place and he isn't there'; the same for oneself; be-odi in Psalm 146:2 read as 'with the little good still in me'; the good points gathered form a melody (niggun).
